title: Nihang speech
hookLine: Nihangs speak in bold, playful coded phrases, like calling one Sikh a hundred and twenty-five thousand

lines: A LONE RIDER: A WHOLE ARMY.
THE DENTED CAR IS THE LIMO.
cards: A lone rider comes into a village and someone asks how many are with him. He grins and says: a whole army. He's alone, and he isn't lying, not by his own way of speaking.
Families do a small version of this. A dented old car gets called the limo. A sandwich at midnight is the feast.
A kid scared of the dark is the brave one. The names aren't mistakes; they're a way of standing up straight. This week brought the shrine keepers, the scholars, the servers and the riders.
It closes with the riders' language.

teach.b: Nihangs have their own way of talking, sometimes called Khalsa bole, the Khalsa's speech, full of bold, playful names for ordinary things.
Tradition says it grew up in the hard years, among riders who had very little, and it turned want into plenty with a word. A plain meal can get a grand name; danger gets a joke for a name.
One well-worn example is the one in today's hook.

teach.h: SAVA LAKH: ONE AS AN ARMY.
teach.b: A single Nihang may call himself sava lakh. Lakh means a hundred thousand; sava means one and a quarter. So one Sikh is a hundred and twenty-five thousand.

teach.h: FEAR NO ONE, FRIGHTEN NO ONE.
teach.b: The phrase comes from a saying tradition puts in Guru Gobind Singh's mouth, in paraphrase: I will make sparrows strike down hawks, and set one to fight a hundred and twenty-five thousand; only then will I be called Gobind Singh.
The speech isn't a boast about strength. It's a refusal to feel small.

teach.h: COURAGE WITH A SMILE ON IT.
teach.b: If you're one, and there are many against you, it says: one is enough. The Guru Granth Sahib keeps that boldness in balance.
In a salok of Guru Tegh Bahadur, in paraphrase: the one who frightens no one, and is frightened of no one, call that one wise. Read the two together.
The bold name is for not being afraid, never for making someone else afraid. A Nihang calling himself an army is standing up straight, not standing over anyone.
And notice the play in it: Nihang speech is funny on purpose, and courage with a smile on it is harder to crush.

games.q: you're a lone rider, and a villager asks how many are with you. in Nihang speech, what do you say?
games.why: one rider can call himself sava lakh: a hundred and twenty-five thousand. not a lie, but a way of standing up straight.

practice: Think of one place where you feel outnumbered, a meeting, a family argument, a task too big for one person, and give yourself a bold, playful name for it, the way a rider would.
Then let Guru Tegh Bahadur's salok ride the breath: in, frighten no one; out, fear no one.
